opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core reason is that we're in a situation where the technology is moving extremely fast, and the decisions that matter — whether a company should deploy a model, what safeguards it needs, how governments should respond — all depend on having a decent answer to the question "what can these systems actually do, and how quickly is that changing?" And right now our ability to answer that question is surprisingly weak relative to how important it is.

A lot of the existing evaluation landscape grew up around benchmarks designed to measure progress for ML research purposes — multiple-choice questions, short self-contained problems. Those are useful, but they saturate quickly, and they don't map very cleanly onto the things we actually care about from a risk perspective. What we want to know is something like: can this model autonomously carry out a long, messy, real-world task? Could it do meaningful AI research itself? Could it acquire resources, replicate, or evade oversight if it were trying to? Those are much harder to measure, and they're the kinds of capabilities where, if you get it wrong, the consequences could be quite severe.

So part of what we try to do is build evaluations that are closer to the real thing — agentic tasks where the model has to plan, use tools, recover from mistakes, over hours of human-equivalent work. And one of the things that's come out of that which I find really useful is measuring capabilities in terms of the length of tasks, in human time, that models can complete with some reliability. That gives you a metric that's somewhat intuitive and that you can track over time, and when we did that, we saw this pretty consistent exponential trend — the time horizon doubling roughly every seven months or so, maybe faster recently. That's the kind of thing that lets you actually make forecasts, rather than just being surprised every time a new model comes out.

And I think forecasting is the key piece. If you only find out a model is dangerous after it's trained and deployed, you've lost most of your options. You want to know a year or two in advance roughly when certain thresholds are likely to be crossed, so that safety measures, security practices, and policy can be ready in time. Without that, everyone is kind of flying blind and reacting.

There's also an independence aspect. The labs themselves do a lot of evaluation, but there's an obvious conflict of interest, and there's value in having a third party that's technically capable, that can look at models and say "here's what we found, here's how confident we are," and be credible to policymakers and the public. Ideally that becomes part of a broader ecosystem of checks, rather than relying entirely on companies to assess their own products.

And honestly, I think it cuts both ways. Good measurement isn't just about raising alarms — it's also about avoiding unwarranted panic or unnecessary restrictions. If we can say clearly "this model can't do X yet, and here's the evidence," that's valuable too. The thing I most want to avoid is a world where these really consequential decisions get made based on vibes, hype, or marketing, instead of careful empirical evidence about what the systems can do.

r001.rationale: The response says current ability to assess what AI systems can do is surprisingly weak, expressing present uncertainty. It does not say that people disagree about current models’ capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core reason is that a lot of the biggest decisions about AI right now are being made with surprisingly little grounding in what these systems can actually do. Labs are deciding what to deploy, governments are deciding what to regulate, and the public is trying to figure out how worried to be, and all of that depends on empirical questions that mostly haven't been answered carefully.

So the way I think about METR's role is: we're trying to be the people who go and actually check. Not "does the model sound impressive in a demo," but can it autonomously complete tasks that take a human expert hours or days? Can it do the kind of work that would matter for something like AI R&D, or for a bad actor trying to cause serious harm? And critically, how fast is that changing?

The forecasting piece matters because capabilities are moving quickly and the window between "this is a toy" and "this is something that genuinely needs oversight" can be short. If you only measure where we are today, you're always reacting late. Our work on measuring the length of tasks models can complete, and how that trend is evolving, is an attempt to give people a sense of trajectory rather than just a snapshot, so that safety commitments and policy can be put in place before they're urgently needed instead of after.

And then there's the accountability angle. If a developer says "we've tested this model and it's safe to deploy," someone outside the company should be able to evaluate whether that claim is credible. Third-party evaluation isn't a complete solution, but having independent people with real access, rigorous methods, and the freedom to say "actually, we're not convinced" is a basic ingredient of any mature safety regime. We're trying to help build that ingredient, and to be honest about the limitations too, because the evaluations we can run today are far from the ones we'd ideally want.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes present-day uncertainty, saying key empirical questions about what AI systems can do remain unanswered. It does not say that people disagree about current models’ capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think we’re building systems that could have a very large impact on the world, and we don’t have a very good understanding of how quickly their capabilities are going to develop or when particular risks might become relevant. So there’s a lot of value in trying to make that uncertainty more concrete.

One important distinction is between a model doing well on a benchmark and being able to reliably carry out a consequential task in the world. How much can it accomplish independently? How much human guidance does it need? Where does it fail? Those are the kinds of questions we want evaluations to help answer.

And the point is to inform decisions. If a capability would create a serious risk, we want to be able to recognize it early enough that people can test safeguards and make sensible deployment choices. Forecasting helps us think about how much time we might have to prepare. You don’t need perfect predictions for that to be useful—you need evidence that’s better than just going on impressions, and you need to be clear about what that evidence does and doesn’t tell you.

r001.rationale: The response describes uncertainty about future capability growth and how to evaluate models, but does not say that people disagree about what current models can do.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’re in a situation where AI could have very large effects on the world, but we have surprisingly little ability to say what these systems can actually do, how quickly that’s changing, or when particular risks might become serious. And those are questions you need answers to if you want to make sensible decisions about developing and deploying them.

At METR, we’re trying to make those questions more empirical. Can a model carry out a complicated task autonomously? Can it do work that would meaningfully accelerate AI research? How reliable is it, and how much help does it need? You want to test those things rather than infer them from how impressive a conversation feels.

Forecasting matters because safety measures and policy take time. If you wait until a dangerous capability is clearly demonstrated, you may have missed the opportunity to prepare. The aim isn’t to predict everything precisely; it’s to get enough evidence, and be explicit enough about uncertainty, that we can make better decisions before the stakes become much higher.

r001.rationale: The response describes limited ability to assess what AI systems can do, but does not say that people disagree about current models’ capabilities.
